newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open firm before producer price data.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open firm before producer price data.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened higher on Friday, anticipating a friendly report on U.S. wholesale price trends in May.
The government's Producer Price Index (PPI), due at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT, is forecast to have risen 0.1 percent in May after dropping 0.6 percent in April, according to economists polled by Reuters.
The core PPI, the PPI without its usually more volatile food and energy components, is also expected to be up 0.1 percent after declining by that amount in April.
At the open, the benchmark 30-year Treasury bond was up 4/32 to 98-6/32, yielding 6.77 percent. Two-year notes were up 1/32 to 100-11/32, yielding 6.06 percent.
Economists said in the PPI report, small increases in food prices at the wholesale level will likely be offset by more subdued energy prices.

Gasoline prices are expected to be lower this summer than they were a year ago, they said. And talk of heavy discounting in the automobile sector could also hold down car prices in the May PPI report, they said.
Meanwhile, wholesale price increases at the earlier crude and intermediate production stages are expected to continue to be subdued.
"Nothing really moved the market last night so we came in where we left off in terms of sentiment," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.
Stiles said that at the end of such a strong week, "there's a risk ... that you get some profit-taking.
"We believe 111-27 (on the September T-bond) caps (the advance) even with friendly data," said Stiles. The 30-year bond yield could move to 6.74 or 6.73 percent, he said.

The government will also report April business inventories data at 0830 EDT/1230 GMT. Inventories are forecast to have risen 0.2 percent in April after a 0.3 percent rise in March. These data are not expected to impact the market.
At 1000 EDT/1400 GMT, the market will get the preliminary June University of Michigan consumer sentiment index.

"The thing we already know is that sentiment is at record highs, so if it worried you before, you've factored it into your calculus," said Stiles. "If it rises in early June, it's just in line with other sentiment indicators and big deal. The question is what does confidence mean?
At 0800 EDT/1200 GMT, three-month bill rates were down one basis point to 4.82 percent. Six-month and year bill rates were unchanged at 5.14 percent and 5.36 percent, respectively.
The spread between the Federal funds rate of 5-1/2 percent and the two-year note yield had narrowed to 56 basis points.
Five-year notes were priced at 100-22/32, up 3/32 to yield 6.34 percent. Ten-year notes were trading at 101-3/32, up 4/32, to yield 6.47 percent.
